title: Dharmakara's primal vow
hookLine: the vow that anyone who calls his name with faith will be born in his land
carry: the door is open: trust and the name

cards: Of all Dharmakara's vows, which one is the door?
Tradition says Pure Land teachers in China and Japan kept circling back to a single vow and gave it a name of its own: the original vow, the root vow, in English often the primal vow.
It doesn't describe jeweled trees or lotus ponds; other vows do that. It answers a plainer question, the one anybody would ask about a wonderful place far away. Who gets in?

teach.b: When I become a Buddha, if beings anywhere in the ten directions entrust themselves to me sincerely and joyfully, wish to be born in my land, and call my name, even ten times, and are not born there, may I not attain perfect awakening.
Same shape as yesterday: if not, not me.

teach.h: WHAT IT ASKS, AND WHAT IT DOESN'T.
teach.b: Second, what it asks, and what it doesn't. Not years on the cushion, a library of sutras, a monastery, money, or a spotless past. Entrusting, wishing, and the name.
The door is set low on purpose. A nurse finishing a night shift can walk through it. So can someone who never learned to read.
You met this door already with Honen and Shinran.
Third, the hard clause. The vow ends with an exception: those who commit the gravest wrongs and slander the teaching. Pure Land teachers have wrestled with that line.

Some read it as a warning meant to keep people from those harms, more than a locked gate. Japanese schools that grew from this vow read it in their own ways, and the coming days will meet them. Fourth, why primal.

In Japanese the word is hongan, the original, root vow. The other vows describe the land; this one opens it. And since the sutra says Dharmakara became a Buddha, Pure Land teachers read the vow as already fulfilled.
In their telling, the door isn't about to open. It's open.

how: Pure Land Buddhists in East Asia treat this vow, hongan in Japanese, as the heart of the longer sutra; they call Amitabha's name, Namu Amida Butsu in Japan or Namo Amituofo in China, trusting that the vow has already been fulfilled.

o: a vow to stay in one temple for the rest of life
a vow monks take on entering a Pure Land temple
his land opened to all who call his name in trust

games.q: the primal vow: tap the pairs.

s: the primal vow requires years of meditation first
it asks for entrusting, wishing for the land, and calling the name.
the vow ends with an exception clause
it names those who commit the gravest wrongs and slander the teaching.
in the vow, the name must be called a thousand times
the vow says even ten times.

games.q: you're Dharmakara, making the vow that decides who can enter your land. what will you ask of them?
o: entrusting themselves, wishing for the land, and calling the name, even ten times.
a whole lifetime without a single fault.
games.why: the vow sets the door low on purpose: entrusting, wishing and the name. no learning, wealth or spotless past required.

practice: Pure Land Buddhists in Japan say Namu Amida Butsu; in China, Namo Amituofo.
If this is your practice, say the name once, slowly and sincerely, and rest; if not, just listen to its sound in your mind, like a neighbor's song through a wall.
Either way, let the breath slow, and stay with the picture of a door offered, not earned.

wordCard.voice: The primal vow. Hongan in Japanese: Dharmakara's vow that those who entrust themselves to him, wish for his land, and call his name will be born there. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: hongan, the original or primal vow. the same characters are read benyuan in Chinese.

carryVoice: Your line: the door is open: trust and the name. No learning, money or spotless past required. That's today.

sources.ref: Larger Sukhavati-vyuha (Sutra of Immeasurable Life), the vow on birth through the name (counted as the eighteenth)
